en: The Record of the Teachings and Practices of the Venerable of Siming, Volume One, with Preface.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zongxiao of Shizhi in Siming.

Preface to the Record of the Teachings and Practices of the Venerable of Siming: The Two National Teachers of the Chen and Sui Dynasties, Tiantai Zhizhe, awakened to the *dhāraṇī* of the revolving *Dharma-puṣpa* (Lotus Sūtra).
He succeeded to the Dharma-nature school and,
with unimpeded eloquence,
analyzed and elucidated the Buddha-vehicle of the three periods of time.
He founded a distinct school of doctrinal and contemplative practice that people have followed to this day. Furthermore,
there exist various ritual manuals for repentance, imperial edicts from two successive dynasties, and stone inscriptions commemorating the construction of monasteries.
His disciple, Chan Master Zhang’an,
compiled these materials into a book titled *The Hundred Records of Guoqing*.
It was especially honored by Emperor Renzong with inclusion in the Tripitaka,
to circulate alongside the Buddhist scriptures; thus,
by this time, there remains almost nothing further to be revealed.
However, the Way and transformation of our ancestors spread throughout sixty provinces;
it flourished during the Sui and Tang dynasties and declined during the Five Dynasties.
The Dharma does not remain eternally obstructed;
the person of ultimate attainment appears for the benefit of others.
During the Tianfu era of the Stone Jin dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Tonggong.
Yitong, whose courtesy name was Huiyitong, came from Goryeo.
He traveled south to visit Luoxi—namely, Dharma Master Huiri of Luoxi Monastery on Mount Tiantai—and mastered the entirety of the Tiantai school’s teachings.
He further desired to cross the sea.
The Great Commander, Master Qian— whose name was Weizhi and who was the son of the King of Wuyue— firmly detained him.
At that time, it was determined that Hongming should reside in Mingzhou.

Consequently, he transmitted the lineage to Hongming at Baoyun Monastery in Mingzhou; this monastery had been established by Gu Chenghui, the Commissioner of Transport for Fuzhou, who donated his own residence to create a temple as a dwelling place for the Master.
The Dharma assembly was grandly opened.
There were two who attained the supernormal power of levitation and left their homes:
the first was the Master of Dharma Wisdom, whose name was Zhili.
The first was Master Ciyun, whose name was Zunshe;
he resided at the Shiyuan Qingsi Monastery and revitalized this teaching.
At that time, he was titled the Venerable of Siming.
Ciyun established the Dharma seat of Mount Ling,
where he stood firm in both understanding and practice.
He was known in the world as the Chan Master of India (Tianzhu).
Ciyun was born in the second year of the Qiande era and passed away at the beginning of the Mingdao era.
After one hundred and twenty years had passed,
his fifth-generation descendant, Master Huiguan,
compiled his surviving writings.
The *Chengjin yuan* (Garden of Accomplished Gold), in three collections,
was circulated in the world.
Fazhi was born in the first year of the Jianlong era.
From the passing of the Sixth Year of the Shengli era until now, one hundred and seventy-five years have elapsed.
The records and excerpts he compiled amount to over three million words.
Scholars collectively venerated him.
Furthermore, there were instructional manuals, doctrinal chapters, question-and-answer sessions, commentaries resolving difficulties, and letters exchanged with eminent scholars and great exegetes;
however, these exist now only as fragmented fragments and scattered remnants, having been lost or dispersed.
Alas! For forty years,
the Master lectured on and transmitted the ritual of repentance with single-minded devotion,
his side never touching the bed.
As for those who have responded by applying their brush to ink,
how could they ever be reckoned by number?
Even if one were to carve them upon wood or stone, [they would remain beyond count].
To record this upon bamboo slips or silk is but one in ten million. I, Zongxiao,
am a disciple of the final age with no talent for emulation.
Having the honor of being enrolled in the school of the Teachings,
I have had the opportunity to privately observe the words bestowed by the Master;
though they consist of but a single phrase or a solitary character, [they are profound].
Since these are all the teachings of the Śākya clan,
how could one allow them to remain neglected and fall into ruin? Thereupon,
he applied himself with great earnestness to seeking them out.
I have obtained only slightly more than one hundred pieces.
Arranged them according to their categories and divided them into seven fascicles,
titling the work *The Record of the Teachings and Practices of the Venerable Master of Siming*.
Siming was the place where he was born, attained the Way, and turned the wheel of Dharma;
the world treasured him as a man,
and all praised him for this reason.
In the Tiantai school, there is no door or window through which one does not establish practice based on the teachings and manifest the teachings through practice;
thus, the two paths of teaching and practice become a single track for cultivation.
The Master once exhorted the assembly, saying:
Whether I am in public or in private,
whether speaking or remaining silent,
I have never failed to take the principles of teaching and contemplation as my sustenance and my staff and rest bench.
I have now compiled this under the title *Teaching through Practice*,
which also reflects the venerable master’s own aspiration.
How magnificent is this work, now completed!
I pray that this may stand as a tripod alongside the *Guoqing Bailu* and the *Tianzhu Jinyuan*,
to be bequeathed to future generations.
This is a shared aspiration for the ancestral Way.
As for that which remains unexhausted,
future sages shall continue it according to their own insights and learning.
This is indeed perfect and excellent.
Written on the day after the full moon of the twelfth month in the second year of Jiatai, the Renxu year, by the Bhikṣu Zongxiao, respectfully.
The Chronological Biography of the Venerable Master. During the reign of Emperor Taizu of the Great Song, when he first ascended the precious throne...
The seventh year of the Zhou Xian-de era was changed to the first year of Jianlong;
this was the gengshen year.
In the first month of this year:
Emperor Taizu received the abdication from Emperor Gong of the Zhou dynasty.
I have carefully consulted the stupa inscription composed by Hu Fang, as well as the *Shilu* (Veritable Record) of his disciple Zequan.
According to these, the Master’s lifespan was sixty-nine years.
He manifested his passing in the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, the Wùchén year.
According to the Record of His Life and Deeds (Xíngyèjì) composed by Duke Zhào Qīngxiàn,
it states that he entered nirvana in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era.
This is an error.
Calculating back from the current *jiǎzǐ* cycle,
the Master’s nativity must have occurred in the *gēngshēn* year.
Is it not the case that true men respond to the destiny of their times, and sages and philosophers appear from time to time?
The Master’s name was Zhili;
his courtesy name was Yuoyan.
The True Sect specially conferred upon him the title of Dharma-Wisdom Great Master (Faxi Dashi).
At that time, he was known as the Venerable of Siming.
His secular surname was Jin.
He was a distant descendant of Jin Midi of the Former Han. The Book of the Western Han states:
"Jin Midi was the son of King Xiutu of the Xiongnu.
When his barbarian nation fell, [he became a hostage]."
He subdued the Han Emperor Wu,
yet remained deeply devoted to loyalty and filial piety,
serving as an inner attendant for seven generations.
Originally, because his ancestor Xiu Tu fashioned a golden man for the purpose of worshipping the Heavenly Lord, he was granted the surname Jin. His descendants later became people of Yin.
His father’s name was Jing.
Her mother was Lady Li.
Initially, as no heir had yet been born,
she sincerely vowed to pray to the Buddha.
Once, in a dream at night,
a Brahman monk gave him a son, saying,
"This is Rāhula."
He was named after this incident.
The second year, *Xinyou*; the third year, *Renxu*; the first year of *Qiande*, *Guihai*; the second year, *Jiazi*; the third year, *Yichou*; the fourth year, *Bingyin*.
At that time, he was seven years old.
The inscription on the stupa states:
"When the Master was seven years old, he encountered the death of his mother."
That is to say, the toil and labor involved are not easily repaid;
moreover, one weeps and wails without ceasing.
It is for this reason that one grows weary of worldly life.
He was in such haste to leave the household life that his father found this extraordinary;
consequently, he did not thwart his resolve.
He first became a disciple of the monk Hongxuan at Taiping Xingguo Temple.
In the preface to the *Shiyao chao* (Essential Excerpts) by his teacher Tianzhu, it says:
"When my master was a youth, he received the scriptures."
He was then able to contemplate its meaning;
his celestial faculties were uniquely awakened.
Is this not what is called the superior nature of one who possesses innate knowledge?

The fifth year, Dingmao; the sixth year, Wuchen; this year was changed to the first year of Kaibao; the second year, Jisi; the third year, Gengwu; the fourth year, Xinwei; the fifth year, Renshen; the sixth year, Guiyou; the seventh year, Jiashu.
At that time he was fifteen years old.
The inscription on his stupa states:
"The Master received full ordination at the age of fifteen."
He specialized exclusively in the Vinaya section. In the eighth year, Jihai, and the ninth year,
Bingzi— this being the year Emperor Taizong ascended the throne and changed the era name to the first year of Taiping Xingguo.
The second year, Dingchou; the third year, Wuyin; the fourth year, Jimao.
At that time, he was twenty years of age.
The *Xingyeji* (Record of Religious Practice) states:
At twenty, he followed Master Baoyun Tong from his native commandery to transmit the practice of Tiantai contemplation.
On the third day, the head seat said to him:
"You should uphold this 'Successive Order of the Dharma Realm' (Dharmadhātu-krama).
The Master asked:
'What is meant by the Dharma Realm?'"
The Master said, "It is this:
the great totality of dharmic characteristics,
perfectly interfused and unimpeded."
The Master said:
"Since it is perfectly interfused and unimpeded,
how could there be any sequence?"
There was no one in the assembly to respond.
After staying for one month,
he himself lectured on the Heart Sūtra.
Everyone was startled by what they heard and spread the news in amazement.
In the fifth year, the Gengchen year, [it occurred].
The Veritable Record states:
While the Master was at Baoyun for two years,
his father happened to have a dream.
He knelt before Tong,
who held a water vessel and poured water into his mouth; from that moment,
the essence of the Perfect and Sudden teaching was realized upon its first reception.
In the sixth year, the Xinsi year,
he was twenty-two years old.
The *Xingye ji* (Record of His Practice) states:
The Master had resided at Baoyun for only three years when he frequently took the place of Master Tong to lecture;
he delved into the texts to elucidate their meanings.
He further elucidated what he had studied.

The seventh year, *Renwu*; the eighth year, *Guiwei*; the first year of *Yongxi*, *Jia Shen*; the second year, *Yi You*; the third year, *Bing Xu*; the fourth year, *Ding Hai*; and the first year of *Duan-gong*, *Wu Zi*.
The Master listened to the reading of the *Ratnamegha-sūtra* for ten years.
This coincided with the passing of his primary lecturer.
The inscription on the stone stupa states:
Tonggong lived to the age of sixty-two.
In the first year of the Duangong era, he passed away.
Zhili and Zunshe were among the most eminent scholars of the *Zijin* [the student body].
The second year, Jichou (489); the third year, Gengyin (490).
In this year, the first year of Chunhua was inaugurated.
The second year, Dingmao (497).
At the age of thirty-two,
the Master was selected by imperial decree to serve as abbot.
The *Shilu* (Veritable Records) states:
In the Xunhua cycle year of Xinmao,
he accepted an invitation at Qianfu Temple and remained there for four years.
At Baoen Yuan,
the words of his precept vow state:
"I dwell at Baoyun."
Having reached the Crane Forest (He-lin), he first moved to a small courtyard on the western side of Qianfu Temple. Qianfu Temple was later renamed Chengtian Temple;
it is now known as Nengren Temple.
The small courtyard on the western side is the present-day Fahua; it has a dormitory but no shrine.
As students moved in and settled there, they numbered over ten, yet there was no room to accommodate them all.
Furthermore, observing that its proximity to the marketplace was truly unsuitable for long-term habitation,
he subsequently moved it to the southeast corner of this city.
The Preface to the *Zhijiao* states:
"When the Master presided over the lecture hall during the Qianfu era,
his disciples followed him with joy."
If the various streams converge into the sea:
the third year, Renchen; the fourth year, Guisi; the fifth year, Jiawu; and the first year of Zhidao, Yiwu; the second year, Bingshen.
The official document states:
In the seventh month of the second year of Zhidao,
the presiding monk of the Inner Court was Julang Xiantong.
He appointed Baoen Yuan and Zhili to serve as the perpetual abbots of the ten directions,
entrusting them to propagate and expound the teachings of Tiantai Master Zhiyi.
The words of the precept vow state:
"In the autumn of the year Bingshen, I inherited this temple;
ten years later, I renovated it."
It was completed in the year Jǐyǒu.
Mr. Shí inscribed it upon stone to record the event.
By the time of Rénzǐ, seventeen years had passed in total.
Hyeom-an came to study.
In the third year, the *dingyou* (1357),
the record of Baoen-yuan states:
Previously, this monastery had been established for many years,
and its dilapidation grew increasingly severe until the third year of the Jōwa era.
He then joined forces with Shi Yiwen of Yuhang to manage the project,
just as he happened to encounter the monk Jueyuan of Danqiu.
He resolved to contribute his strength,
and after three years, the labor was completed.
Beholding the magnificence of its architecture, one sees the gold and green glinting together in radiant splendor.
The Buddha Hall comes first and the Sangha Hall follows,
manifesting the proper order.
The scriptural library is on the right and the Abbot’s quarters are on the left.
It was thus convenient for the matter at hand.
When Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne, he changed the era name to Xianping.
The first year was Wuxu.
The second year, Jihai (479).
At that time, he was forty years of age.
The Shilu (Veritable Record) states:
From the second year of the Xianping era onwards, the Master devoted himself exclusively to lecturing on and performing repentance rites;
he remained constantly seated and did not lie down to sleep.
His feet never ventured outside;
all requests for audiences were sent away.
In the third year, the Gengzi year.
In that year there was a great drought.
The Master, together with the Indian *kṣāntivādin*, prayed for rain and was moved by divine response.
The *Xingye ji* states:
In that year, there was a great drought.
The Master, together with Zunshe, jointly practiced the *Guangming* Repentance,
praying for rain for approximately three days.
Without descending, he naturally used one hand to provide for the Buddha;
before the Buddhist rites were concluded,
the rain had already soaked everything thoroughly.
The *Ciyun Xingye Ji* (Record of the Deeds of Ciyun) states:
In the third year of the Xiānpíng era,
there was a great drought in Sìmíng.
The Master entered into a ritual of repentance and prayed for rain for three days,
vowing that if it did not rain, he would immolate himself.
When the result manifested exactly as predicted,
the Prefect Su marveled at this marvel and inscribed the event upon a stone to record it.
The fourth year, Xinchou; the fifth year, Renyin; the sixth year, Gui Mao.
In this year, a Japanese National Preceptor dispatched a monk to pose difficult questions.
The original preface states:
In the sixth year of the Xianping era,
the year of Gui Mao (1003 CE),
the Japanese monk Jikishō and others brought twenty-seven questions concerning points of divergence regarding the Tiantai teachings from Zen Master Yuankui of Mount Tiantai in their own country.
In the first year of the Jingde era (Jiachen), Zhi Li of Siming provided brief answers based on the teachings,
recording them as they were requested.
At the age of forty-five,
he composed the *Essential Commentary on the Ten Non-dual Gates* (*Shibu’ermen zhiyao chao*),
in the preface of which he recorded the year and month.
Preface written on the ninth day of the first month of the first year of Jingde (Jiachen). The second year was Yisi;
the third year was Bingwu.
In this year, the Master presented the "Ten Treatises on the Meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra" to the Duke of Zhao at Qiandang.
Preface: In the fourth month of the third year of the Jingde era,
Mingli of the Four Wisdoms Temple.
With a sincere mind for the sake of the Dharma,
I questioned the meaning [of the text] with the Venerable Master Zhao of Zhiyang in the fourth year, Dingwei.
In this year, [the Emperor] presented his "Two Hundred Questions on Contemplating the Mind" (*Guānxīn èrbǎiwèn shū*).
The preface states:
"The fourth year of the Jingde era."
The monk Zhili of Siming,
with a sincere heart dedicated to the Dharma,
respectfully inquired about the meaning [of these matters] from the Lecturer Zhao of Zheyang.
In the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, Wushen (564 CE), and the second year, Jiyou (565 CE),
when he was fifty years of age,
the Bao'en Cloister was completed.
The words of the precept vow state:
"The temple was completed in the year of Jihou (1719).
Master Shi recorded this."
The postscript states:
"I have waited for inquiries regarding the bamboo tally and the official seal, and have personally examined the pine handle;
now that this temple has reached the completion of its work, I record this."
He then took up his brush to compose this inscription.
It was established on the sixth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, the Jiyou year (1009 CE).
In the third year, the Gengxu year (1010 CE).
In this year, in accordance with the Imperial Decree,
the name of Ba'en was changed to Yanqing Monastery.
According to the *Sijimingtu jing* (Illustrated Scripture of the Four Ming Mountains),
Ba'en Yuan was established in the second year of the Zhou Guangshun era.
During the third year of the Daizhong Xiangfu era of the Imperial Dynasty, it was renamed Yanqing Yuan.
In the fourteenth year of the Xiangshu era, the temple was upgraded from an *yuan* to a *si*.
The official decree stated:
"In the seventh month of the third year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era..."

The internal monk Zhili submitted a formal petition to the Prefectural Government, requesting that it be presented to the Imperial Majesty so that he might permanently serve as the abbot for the ten directions.
He lectured extensively on the Tiantai teachings.
In the tenth month of that year,
he received an official memorandum from the Chancellery.
In accordance with the Imperial Edict,
it was granted. In the fourth year,
the Xinhai year, the Master again submitted a formal petition through the prefecture requesting its bestowal.
The memorial dispatch states that the aforementioned imperial edict be fully recorded and engraved upon stone for perpetual reference.
The dispatch reads:
In the third month of the fourth year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era,
Zhili submitted a formal petition from within the prefecture,
requesting that the imperial edict and the preceding and succeeding official dispatches be transcribed in full.
This was engraved upon a stone stele to serve eternally as the abiding foundation for the transmission of the teachings throughout the ten directions.
On the seventeenth day of the seventh month of this year.
The edict was issued and a stone stele erected in the fifth year, the Renzi year.
In this year, the Master [Donggwang] and Master Iwon...
I have composed this "Vow for the Abbot of the Ten Directions Teaching Lineage" to be inscribed upon stone as a perpetual warning against the irrational and arbitrary seizure of property.
This text is truly the fundamental basis for the abbots of the ten directions throughout ten thousand generations of this monastery.
In the sixth year, the year of Gui-chou (1693),
on the fifteenth day of the second month of this year,
he established the Nianfo Shijie Assembly (the Assembly for the Bestowal of Precepts through Buddha-recitation).
In the tenth month of the fifth year of the Xiangfu era,
the Master personally composed this memorial text,
which continues to inspire and transform others to this day.
From that time until now, this assembly has not ceased for a total of one hundred and ninety years.
As for those who have been transformed by its influence throughout past and present,
one cannot know how many there may be.
In the seventh year, the Jia-yin year,
he composed the *Rongxin jie* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra for Melting the Mind).
At the end of the preface, it is inscribed:
Preface on the Double Ninth Day of the Jia-yin year, the seventh year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era.
In this same year, the Master also composed the *Seven Chapters of Miscellaneous Questions on the Teachings*, to which his disciple Ziren provided the responses. The eighth year was the Yi-mao year.
In the ninth year, the Bingchen year,
at the age of fifty-seven.
The Shilu (Veritable Record) states:
The Master was fifty-seven years old when he vowed to practice the Lotus Repentance. After three years,
his period of repentance was completed.
He performed the offering of self-immolation to honor this sublime sutra,
vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
This was in the first year of the Tianxi era, the Ding-si year.
The epitaph states:
At the beginning of the first year of the Tianxi era,
the Master had reached the age of sixty.
He then said to his disciples:
"For half a verse, one lost his body;
for a single phrase, one threw himself into the fire."
The mind of the Sage toward the Dharma is thus.
That I am unable to sacrifice my own body and life in order to rouse myself from indolence—
how can this even be mentioned?
Thereupon, ten monks were assembled to perform the Lotus Repentance for three years;
when the repentance was complete, they burned themselves together.
At that time, Yang Yi, the Hanlin Academician,
and Li Zunxu, the Prince Consort,
were both preeminent literary figures and men of great merit at court.
Whenever he heard that Master Xiang had attained profound realization,
he would invariably admire him from afar.
In that year, an imperial edict granted him a purple *kāṣāya*.
All of these were positions bestowed through the recommendations of the two gentlemen.
Furthermore, I have heard that he was prepared to sacrifice his life,
and thus Lord Yang sent him a letter.
He earnestly entreated him to remain in the world for a long time;
after several rounds of such exchange,
he finally entrusted the regional governor with the task of providing protection.
Consequently, his vows and practices could not be fulfilled, and he bestowed [his teachings] upon others.
Furthermore, he composed the "Chapter on Subduing the Three Usages" and produced the "Thirty Questions from the Crimson Curtain."
The disciple Rengegaku replied, "All [these events] are recorded in this year:
the second year, Wumwu; the third year, Jiyiwei; and the fourth year, Gengshen."
The Veritable Records state:
In the fourth year of the Tianxi era,
the Prince Consort Li Zunxü...
He submitted a record of his life’s achievements to the throne,
which resulted in the special bestowal of the title "Dharma-Wisdom Great Master" (Fazhi Dashi).
In that same year, twenty-three eminent figures from the monastic offices of the capital [were also honored].
Each was assigned a poem to commemorate and present to the Master.
Chao Shuo-ze, the Court Attendant, composed a preface for it and had it engraved on stone.
Later, Zhe-lin titled his poem as follows:
Written on the full moon day of the last month of autumn in the year Gengshen.
The fifth year, Xinyou;
at that time, [the author] was sixty-two years of age.
In that year, the Imperial Court issued a decree bestowing upon him the mandate to compose the *Sankan-hō* (Repentance Ritual).
The *Gyōgyōki* states:
"The Emperor Shōzō [True Ancestor] was aware of the Master’s reputation."
An imperial eunuch was dispatched to his residence with orders to perform the Lotus Sūtra Repentance Rite,
and he was granted generous rewards.
The eunuch was Yu Yuanqing.
Because Master Yu wished to understand the essential meaning of the method of repentance,
[the Master] recounted for him the core principles of practicing repentance.
People to this day continue to receive his bounty.
He also compiled the *Separate Commentary on the Profound [Commentary]* (*Bie xing xuanshu ji*),
the title of whose preface reads:
On the first day of the eighth month in the fifth year of the Tianxi era,
he further composed the *Miaozong Chao* (Excerpts on the Wondrous Pivot) of the *Amitābha Sūtra*,
the preface of which is titled:
Preface written on the Double Ninth of the fifth year of Tianxi.
The first year of Qianxing was Renxu, and the second year was Guihai.
It was in this year that Emperor Renzong ascended the throne.
In the first year of the Kaisheng era,
in that same year, he composed the *Giming Shiyiji* (Supplementary Record of the Radiant Light).
The record states:
Preface on the full moon day of the fourth month in the first year of the Tiānshèng era.
The Master also composed a colophon for Pán Tūntián’s "Dream Fish."
Furthermore, he produced the *Wenwei* (Inquiries from the Screen) to test the forty-two chapters and examine his disciples.
He also provided answers to the Ten Questions on the Buddha-Dharma posed by Master Tai of the Chan School. The second year, Jiazi.
The third year, the year of Yichou (1025),
during the early Tianxi era of Emperor Zhenzong,
an imperial edict was issued for the establishment of *fangsheng chi* (pools for the release of living beings) throughout the empire.
The Master, wishing to broaden the sacred transformation,
would every year on the Buddha’s birthday solicit the assembly to perform the practice of releasing living beings.
Thereupon, a stele for the release of living beings was erected.
Liu Yun, Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, composed the inscription;
Zeng Hui, Palace Secretary and Governor, set up the stone.
Written by the monk Renyue of Xixi on the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the third year of the Tiansheng era.
That year, one night, the Master suddenly dreamed.
The Official entered the monastery.
On the following day, the son of Grand Guardian Zeng arrived;
subsequently, it indeed accorded with this dream.
This was Duke Xuanjing of the state of Lu.
Consequently, Lady Huang of the state of Chu established permanent endowments to provide for the community.
Furthermore, she submitted a memorial to Governor Zeng, requesting that he petition the throne for the land of the rear garden.
The Yongzai Monastery was also established in this same year.
The fourth year was Bingyin.
In this year, the Master bestowed his final instructions upon his disciple Wen Can;
the stone inscription still exists.
In the fifth year, Dingmao.
The Master composed the *Wenju Ji* (Record of the Phrases and Sentences) in six fascicles.
He dated this work the third day of the second month in the fifth year of the Tiānshèng era.
However, this record was completed as the Master was pressed by the approach of his passing into nirvana.
Before the volume was completed,
the later disciple, Dharma Master Guangzhi Shangxian,
continued the record by adding the chapter on Praising the Buddha.
This was then established as the definitive original text.
In the sixth year, the Wuchen year (828 CE),
the Master, at the age of sixty-nine, manifested his passing into extinction.
According to the *Shilu* (Veritable Records) and other sources,
at the hour of Wu on the fifth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era,
the Master sat upright in the full lotus posture.
Having finished preaching the Dharma to the assembled multitude,
he suddenly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha several hundred times and then passed away in an instant.
He revealed his body from within the open niche;
after two weeks had passed,
both his nails and hair had grown long.
His countenance remained as if alive.
After another seven days had passed,
he was moved outside the southern gate.
When he was about to be cremated,
first a fragrant and rich aroma was perceived;
when the fire was extinguished, his tongue was found intact.
The śarīra were of five colors and their number was unknown.
They were enshrined within a lapis lazuli bottle and installed atop the Daibekkaku (Hall of Great Compassion). Five years passed.
On the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Mingdao era,
his remains were enshrined and a stupa was erected to the left of Chongfa Monastery.
Zongxiao has humbly read the *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Monks) of the Three Dynasties;

Zhiyi of Siming, in his preface,

The second question:

In the Commentary, the specific presentation that the poison of principle is not inherently evil—

if it is inconceivable, [then...]

Question Eight:

He then said:

This refers to using divine mantras to treat poison.
Does this statement mean that it is subjugated by the principle of reality (*dharmatā*),

However, based on the principle of the unchanging following conditions,
the three teachings of Final, Sudden, and Perfect have been established.
I request that you explain in detail the principles of these three teachings and the manner in which they follow conditions.
If there were no distinct characteristics,
how could the three teachings be established?
If there were distinct characteristics, [how could they be established]?
"Please explain this in detail.
(The fifth question:

"Since the commentaries on the *Treatise on the Five Teachings* do not yet discuss the inherent presence of all dharmas within the fundamental nature of reality according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)."
Is this comparable to the attainment of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) of the present school?
Compared to the Perfect [Teaching] of that [other school], even the present Perfect Teaching is as vastly different from it as heaven is from earth.
The principle of the teachings for those nearing the end of life is equal to that of the present Perfect [Teaching].
Question Six:
The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the *Zhiguan*) does not discuss the principle as being replete with all phenomena (*liju zhufa*).
Is it because you know but do not speak,
or because you do not know?
If it is because you know but do not speak, then...
This would entail the fault of obscuring profound meanings;
if one does not understand them from the outset,
then one is unskilled in expounding the Perfect [Teaching].
How could it be the same as the present Perfect [Teaching]?
That Perfect [Teaching] is already not the same as the present Perfect;
how much less so the Final Teaching?
Seventh question:
Since the *Zangshu* does not yet discuss the principle as being replete with all phenomena,
it follows that a single principle transforms according to conditions to produce all phenomena.
Thus, it is not that there is no unconditioned activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*). If unconditioned activity were not established,
how could it be identical to the perfection [of the present]?
Question Eight:

The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Storehouse) states that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) speaks of the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), wherein the primary and its attendants are interpenetrating in layers.
This resembles the present meaning of how the Middle Way among form, fragrance, and all other phenomena tends toward form and so forth.
Discussing this in comparison,
it seems similar to the present Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Could that Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) maintain such a statement as "the unchanging follows conditions" (bùbiàn suíyuán)?
If one speaks of the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena,
this is precisely that Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
not the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao).
If one has not yet attained such [realization],
how could one even hope to equal that perfection,
let alone achieve the current perfection?
Question Nine:
Regarding the doctrine of the final teaching (*zhongjiao*) on "the unchanging following conditions" (*bùbiàn suíyuán*),
how does it compare with the "unchanging following conditions" elucidated in the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel)?
Are they the same or different?
If they are different,
then it is not the present perfection.
If they are the same, the *Jinbi* explains that true thusness is the myriad dharmas because it accords with conditions.
All phenomena are true thusness (tathatā),
because they are unchanging;
this is based on these two meanings.
It establishes that insentient things possess Buddha-nature.
Although the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) establishes that [the nature] is unchanging while following conditions, it says:
When present in sentient beings, it is called buddha-nature;
when present in insentient things, it is called only dharma-nature and is not called buddha-nature.
Since the two schools have already diverged,
to claim that they are "unchanging" is precisely what constitutes "change."
Since this already contradicts the *Golden Needle*,
how can it be called the "perfect principle"?
One must understand that in the provisional teachings, there is the name but not the meaning.
Because the statement regarding the existence of Buddha-nature is spoken in terms of both provisional expedients and ultimate principle,
and since it is not yet said to be "pervasive" in terms of either expedient or principle,
what else could this be but a provisional teaching?
The Ten Questions.
The *Jinbi* (Golden Needle) says:
A guest asked:
Why is it that the provisional teachings do not state that the two causes—conditions and fulfillment—are universal?
I reply: because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have conceived of a self and what belongs to a self.
Judging from what has been indicated,
it should not yet be said that [the teaching] is universal;
in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the ultimate truth is taught while retaining provisional means.
Therefore, emptiness can be used as an analogy for the "correct" (the principal),
but it cannot yet serve as an analogy for the "conditions" and "completion.
If the teaching were exclusively provisional, [it would be insufficient].
Thus, the three causes are all restricted;
just as the initial hearing of the correct teaching by those of separate capacities is restricted,
so it is for the nature of the treasury and the rational nature in all cases.
Therefore, although it is widely heard that insentient things do not exist,
based on delusion, one points out delusion,
saying that they are capable of creating [the world].
The appended "Establishment of Nature Based on Authority" states that what is produced is not superior; all is like a golden needle, with not a single character moved.
Second, the two causes are not pervasive.
It is further said that while the provisional carries authority,
the true realm possesses sentience; thus,
they definitively belong to distinct categories.
Since the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) is thus,
why do you insist that it is the Perfect Teaching (Yuan)?
Question Eleven.
The Tibetan commentaries clearly judge the ālayavijñāna to be the basis for the arising of phenomena; therefore, it is termed the "divisive teaching" (fenjiao).
This reveals that True Suchness (tathatā) is the basis for the arising of phenomena, which is thus termed the "ultimate teaching" (zhongjiao).
Since you now believe that the distinct principle of non-abiding can produce all phenomena, [you have understood this].
If one does not follow conditions,
how could one possibly create dharmas?
(The twelfth question.)
No other school asserts that there is no abiding.
You now provide a forced interpretation of the *dharmatā* upon which you rely, attempting to equate it with non-abiding.
Even if you were to offer such a forced interpretation, [it would still be incorrect].
As for the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), which holds that the True [Mind] follows along with delusion to construct all phenomena—
is this not a principle that can be overturned?
If it cannot be overturned, [then how so?]
Can conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) be said to possess the mutual interpenetration of the one and the many, such that all things are mutually unimpeded?
If so, how does this differ from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)?
If it were not so, what would "non-concealment" (anāvaraṇa) be?
Could it be that the nature of reality (tathatā-dharmatā) itself lacks sovereignty?
It should be understood that in the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), it is solely principle (li) because of its non-abiding nature;
thus, one must not cling to the nature of the Buddha-realm,
for that would constitute being fettered by delusion.
It is pressed down to form the nine realms;
this precisely accords with the meaning of being "capable of being covered.
Those who receive this teaching [should understand it thus].
Although one may believe that True Suchness transforms and creates all phenomena,
one does not yet know that each phenomenon is perfectly interfused within its own locus.
This is because this teaching has not yet elucidated how the principle of nature is inherently and instantaneously endowed with all phenomena.
If one receives this present perfect teaching,
having realized that the nature-virtues inherently possess all dharmas,
even though they undergo transformation and construction through ignorance, [they remain as such].
It is thus both created and uncreated,
because it is inherently complete and because phenomena are identical with principle.
The Dharmadhātu is perfectly constant and universally encompasses all phenomena;
there is nothing that is not the Dharmadhātu.
Since this is not the case for that which is expounded by the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), [it cannot be so].
How could that be equal to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) of the present?
Question Thirteen:
The Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) states that True Suchness (Tathatā) is Original Enlightenment (Benjue).
The Separate Teaching states that True Suchness is the Buddha-nature.
Is this nature not fundamental?
Is the Buddha not awakening?
Since names and meanings are already in accord,
how could they not be identical?
The fourteenth question.
The Yogācāra school asserts that because True Suchness (tathatā) lacks cognition, it cannot be deluded;
the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) maintains that because True Suchness possesses cognition, it can be deluded.
Because it is capable of delusion, it is capable of awakening;
therefore, it is established as "following conditions.
Since there is distinct principle within this, there is awareness and cognition.
Is it not possible for that to be so?
If it were possible,
would it not then follow conditions?
Question Fifteen:
The Master said,
"A separate principle that is non-abiding can create all dharmas."
If it is merely that principle can create phenomena,
which is a sense of partiality,
then is it not the case that there is only the meaning of following conditions and lacks the meaning of non-change?
Master Yuan did not realize that if one does not understand "unchanging," then the ultimate teaching and the differentiated teachings would share the same exposition.
If one follows conditions, then [the doctrine of] "following conditions" exists solely within the ultimate teaching.
Therefore, it is clarified that being unchanging does not necessarily entail following conditions.
If one speaks of following conditions,
there must necessarily be an unchanging aspect,
because it is the nature of True Suchness that follows conditions.
If it changes according to conditions,
then it cannot be called "nature.
Question sixteen.
The Master said:
"The Separate Teaching (biejiao) says they are not identical;
the Final Teaching (zhongjiao) speaks of their identity."
As for those who hold differing views,
it is because they are deluded regarding names and fail to investigate the principle thoroughly;
for they do not discuss the inherent presence of the nine realms within nature.
This refers to the principle alone following conditions to manifest as nine;
if ignorance is severed,
these nine realms must necessarily be destroyed.

If the nine realms are themselves the principle of True Suchness (tathatā), the general meaning is that both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* explain it according to this principle, as in such statements as "the initial mind is the subsequent mind," and so forth.
Why is it necessary to eliminate nine?
Is it not the case that the nine meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are capable of obstructing the principle (tattva)?
If you say this is not so, [then explain].
Does the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) also state that the nine realms are all the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), with each one universally encompassing the others?
If it does, how does it differ from the Perfect Teaching (Yuan)?
If one does not speak [of this],
how can one claim [to understand] the ultimate truth?
This is especially so since that Perfect Teaching has not yet discussed the inherent possession of the three thousand [dharmas].
Although it is said that each [category] encompasses [all things],
there is as yet no reason why they should encompass them all.
If compared with the present perfect [system], [the former is incomplete].
This is not even established in the sense of the *Yogācāra* school,
let alone in the *Niṣṭhānirvāṇa* (Final) Teaching.
Question Seventeen.
The Master said:

"To claim that the nine realms are inherently complete within the nature (*prakṛti*) yet cannot be called 'distinct' is because one has not understood that within the principle itself there is the meaning of establishing all phenomena."
Therefore, the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) states:
"Principle consists of the inherent virtues of the conditions and the understanding.
Furthermore, if one were to claim that the various phenomena inherently contained within nature cannot be called "differentiated," [it would be a fallacy].
For what reason does the *Commentary on the Wondrous Sutra* state:
"If one knows that the earth possesses both peaches and plums,
one then recognizes that within the real there is the provisional"?
To understand non-differentiation as itself differentiation is to know that when one perceives the verticality of peaches and plums,
one recognizes the reality within the provisional.
The differentiation of understanding is itself non-differentiation.
Since the earth is provisionally designated as possessing peaches and plums,
this provisional designation is called "differentiation."
Is it not the case that the nine realms are called "distinct" precisely because they are intrinsically complete within the nature?
(Question 18) Regarding the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*) of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening.
Citing the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, he takes the principle-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
My view is that if this passage is taken as proof for the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), [it would contradict the established tenets].
This refers to the meaning of "following conditions.
If one realizes the Separate Teaching (biejiao),
it does not have the meaning of "following conditions."
Furthermore, the citation here is abbreviated;
that sutra states in full:
"The seven consciousnesses do not circulate."
The ignorance that does not act as the cause of suffering or pleasure is empty in essence;
the Tathāgatagarbha, however, acts as the cause for both the wholesome and the unwholesome,
whether in arising or in ceasing.
Experiencing suffering and pleasure,
it co-arises with its causes as the suchness that accomplishes phenomena;
being thus able to act as a cause.
Furthermore, regarding the passage on "arising and ceasing," how can it be interpreted as not following conditions?
If you claim that passages such as those concerning arising and ceasing do not follow conditions because they are not cited [as examples], [that is incorrect].
Furthermore, within the Vijñaptimātra school,
can it be said that True Suchness (tathatā) is the cause of good and evil?
Moreover, the subsequent passage employs the analogy of the pond water from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra.
How is this to be reconciled?
Therefore it is said:
"It is like the water of a great pool."
When an elephant enters, it becomes turbid;
when a pearl enters, it becomes clear.
One should know that the water of the pond is the basis for both clarity and turbidity.
Since the pearl and the elephant lack the conditions for being clear or turbid,
I now ask:
does the water in the pond become clear or turbid in accordance with these two conditions?
If one follows [the conditions],
how can one form an interpretation that does not follow those conditions?
This is the nineteenth question.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains the arousal of the mind according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), stating:
"Within the afflictions lies the Tathāgatagarbha;
ordinary beings, like those born blind, are constantly accompanied by this garbha."
Yet they do not know or see this;
thus they wander through birth and death,
and are instead harmed by their own storehouse consciousness.
Furthermore, since Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (biejiao) resolve their minds upon seeing sentient beings as they truly are,
how could one say that True Suchness (tathatā) does not conform to conditions?
This is the twentieth question.
The Master said:
"The essential point is that, because [the opponent] raised a question based on the premise established by National Teacher Huian,
he specifically set forth a distinct principle regarding 'following conditions' (suiyuan)."
Gai Zi did not understand the meaning of An Guo’s question,
which led to this erroneous statement.
As his question states:
In the Separate Teaching (biejiao), True Suchness does not follow conditions;
in the *Awakening of Faith*, True Suchness is able to follow conditions.
I do not yet know whether the *Awakening of Faith* belongs to the Separate Teaching or the Perfect Teaching (yuan).
If they were distinct,
the text would be contradictory; if they were identical,
[it would be redundant].
This deviates from that commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Regarding the initial statement concerning "conforming to conditions" (*suiyuan*) versus "not conforming to conditions":

this was likely intended for those superficial scholars who falsely claim that the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) does not discuss conforming to conditions, when in fact it does speak of conforming to conditions.
Following common sense, he poses the question;
since it is already commonly known that the *Awakening of Faith* discusses how True Suchness (tathatā) accords with conditions,
he therefore determines the matter as follows:
It is not yet clear whether this meaning of "following conditions" (suiyuan) is distinct or perfect.
This is because those who study superficially do not realize that the principle of True Suchness following conditions applies to both teachings.
Therefore, I shall now define both.
The subsequent formal objection states:
If it is claimed that the *Awakening of Faith* is a separate [work],
this would first contradict the treatise itself.
According to the treatise, the single mind subsumes both mundane and supramundane phenomena as well as the "greatness of characteristics.
This clarifies that it possesses immeasurable inherent qualities and virtues,
because it is fundamentally endowed with the thousand suchnesses (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, the eight aspects of the ten stages belong to the partial truth of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao),
because they represent the spontaneous and effortless manifestation of response within the stages of the Perfect [Teaching].
If one were to definitively categorize them as belonging solely to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao), it would be incorrect.
This would contradict this passage from the *Śāstra*.
If one were to definitively judge it as belonging to the Perfect [Teaching],
it would deviate from the *Commentary* by Fazang.
In this commentary, the fact that the mind inherently possesses the hundred realms (*śata-dhātu*)— which encompasses both mundane and supramundane phenomena—
and the immeasurable qualities of nature are not explained by means of the categories of "inherently good" and "inherently evil."
Furthermore, the eight marks of the tenth stage are not explained as being "partially true" (fenzhen),
but rather it is stated that they are produced by the power of vows and supernormal faculties while dwelling in the subduing of the afflictions of views and thoughts (jiansi).
If these were judged to belong to the Perfect Teaching (yuan), [such an explanation would be inconsistent].
This would contradict such passages in the *Śāstra*.
If you now maintain that An-guo’s definitive judgment— that the Final Teaching (zhōngjiào) is the present Perfect Teaching (yuán)— is correct,
for what reason do you raise the formal objection as follows?
If Yuan [Tsung-tao] deviates from that *Zangshu*,
then the *Zangshu* must be correctly employing the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*) to explain the *Awakening of Faith*.
If the Final Teaching is indeed the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), then...
If one explains it as being "perfectly round" (circular),
this precisely accords with the *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Storehouse).
How could it be said that explaining it as "perfectly round" contradicts that *Zangshu*?

Verses on the Questions and Answers from the "Chapter on the Essential Substance" of the *Fahua Xuanyi*. Questioned by the Repentance Master Ciyun, Answered by the Dharma Master of Siming, Zunshe, who bows his head to the Dharma Lord of Yanqing.
I have heard that recently you have been eloquently expounding the profound Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
Reflecting upon this myself, I think:
I am bound by circumstances and have no opportunity to occupy this seat.
Furthermore, regarding the profound meaning of this sutra, it shows that the title is derived from its essential substance as the fifth point;
this intent is subtle and profound.
I have pondered this for many nights without reaching a resolution.
I have therefore respectfully composed these verses to present for your consideration and guidance.
I pray that you will explain this externally for my sake;
I look forward with eager anticipation to the arrival of your reply.
What is this "dharma-nature"? Is its essence the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light), or is it established according to its meaning?
Is it established by way of substance, or is dharma-nature fundamentally not substantial? From what does this golden color arise?
If established according to their meaning, they are still merely provisional names.
When the entire gold is the Dharma-realm, every atom is entirely equal.
What is extinguished by repentance? What is glorified by praise?
Since sin and merit are not two, emptiness is but a hollow sound;
The treasury of emptiness is fully manifest as emptiness, and the earth-treasury is as difficult to overturn as the earth itself.

The Lotus and the Weed: How should one evaluate their essence?
They are identical in principle to all dharmas. May the Lion’s String vibrate with resonance.
With respect, I prostrate to the Master of the Ling Shan Repentance.
Following his example, we have observed the retreat of the feet and engaged in the study of the scriptures;
though our realization of the Way is not yet profound,
these time-honored maxims remain ever-present.
I have now received this inquiry from Your Majesty,
which arises from great compassion and impels me to investigate.
I have caused others to attain realization;
however, due to the busyness of worldly affairs,
I have long been unable to offer my gratitude.
I now offer this reply in full;
I trust you will examine it closely.
The Dharma-nature possesses all forms, which are termed "subtle and wondrous forms."
The Dharma-nature possesses all meanings, and is thus called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
How could this meaning and this form be divided into two natures?
Fire is itself true emptiness; the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies this intent.
The nature of form is itself the nature of wisdom; The *Awakening of Faith* clarifies its ultimate intent.
The myriad aspects of the *tathatā* are both with and without marks;
Only within a single instant can they be entrusted to the principle of emptiness and non-emptiness. Only then does Vairocana pervade all places.
Exhausting all forms down to the subtlest atoms is the primordial ground;
investigating the mind-vow for a single instant is true suchness-wisdom.
The nose smells the fragrance of merit; the tongue tastes the flavor of the sublime Dharma.
That the characteristics of the world appear as permanent is truly due to abiding in the station of dharmas;
that the Dharma-body flows through the five paths is truly due to possessing expedient means and wisdom.
When the mind is deranged, gold and stone become obscured; when afflicted by the disease of form, one is intoxicated by conceptual thoughts.
Mind and form are non-different in principle; how could their substance and meaning ever diverge?
Sentient beings are deluded regarding the fundamental source, yet they firmly distinguish between the vessel and its contents.
Relying on emptiness, one performs repentance and praise; the essence of the dharma-realm is fully present.
The radiance illuminates the world; the true gold is the most precious among all dharmas.
The ultimate reality-body manifests and summons that which cannot be compared, striking forth this profound mystery.
I know that you are fully endowed with the two adornments.
Having made this assessment, I again request that you refine and polish it.
I shall further present it in verse to my Dharma elder,
Yanqing, for his perusal.
I still await your reply.
Regarding the fourfold silence of *nirvāṇa*: it is because of causes and conditions that characters are established;
furthermore, it is said that in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there are words and there is real meaning.
Existence and non-existence, the ultimate and the conventional—how are their similarities and differences distinguished?
All phenomena are themselves suchness; they have no names and no characters.
Suchness itself is all phenomena; they appear with differences according to conditions.
Arising necessarily consists of the three thousand [realms];
how could one not say that the natures of water and fire are empty of reality? Who can distinguish between unity and difference within emptiness?
They manifest according to karma, diverging from the end toward their respective destinations.
The establishment [of phenomena] arises entirely from conventionality;
why then should one not say that the nature of form (*rūpa*) is itself the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*)?
This is because their essence is non-dual—there is neither duality nor non-duality, neither right nor wrong—and this is the primordial ground itself.
Yet one must wait until even the subtlest atoms (*paramāṇu*) are exhausted; only then can it be said how wisdom is revealed.
Fundamentally, there is but one refined clarity, which divides into six kinds.
Though the provisional means (*upāya*) have many gates, the nature that returns to the source is non-dual.
Non-duality is suchness itself; how could there be a correspondence between the natures of fragrance, flavor, medicine, and disease?
When the mind and form employ skillful means to treat water and fire, each rising or sinking, they suddenly fall into discord and abandonment.
Dependent origination arises solely from nature; how could it manifest as non-dual?
All phenomena are like a great illusion: the one and the many mutually rely on each other as their substance, and the illusory is itself the real. Why labor to distance oneself from them both?
Dust has been exhausted and moments forgotten; how can there still be the intention of existence or non-existence?
When observing the mind, at first I could not endure it; why is it that now I can endure this intention?
Though the act of accepting or rejecting rests with me, I remain hesitant for the time being.
The Great Teacher of Gods and Humans: Why is it that there is no definitive wisdom?
To contemplate the mind is also to contemplate form;
if one contemplates only the ground of the mind, this is not called contemplating the mind, for there is no meaning of the mind that is not all-encompassing.
Regarding identity and difference, and their mutual inclusion—how can one grasp their intended meaning?
Contemplating the mind as being but a single thought-moment, within that single thought-moment the three thousand realms are complete;
these three thousand realms encompass both the body and the land. Yet, [the verse] alone omits the principle of contemplating form.
Regarding the three thousand worlds and external objects, how can one attain uniformity?
With reverence for ritual and propriety, I have humbly set forth my foolish thoughts.
This is my second response to the questions posed by the Master of the Ling-shan Repentance Rite.
I hope you will deign to examine this:
The single ultimate truth of *nirvāṇa*—whether as negation or affirmation—is not a matter of difference;
whether expressed through words or transcending words, it is entirely the meaning of *tathatā*.
This is the conventional and this is the real; that which is non-sentient follows wisdom.
Both truths are called "real. This reality has names;
if one realizes its nature as the three thousand [worlds], this is the meaning of *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature).
All phenomena are ultimately true and eternal; both name and reality are noble.
If one relies on these partial and conceptualized dharmas, how can they be taken as a standard?
Their essence is like flowers in the sky; what reality could there be in their names?
Mind and form are non-dual in essence; within the emotions, there is a stubborn attachment to difference.
To break this stubborn emotional attachment, one must push to the ultimate limit.
If one knows the treasury of the underlying principle, not a single phenomenon will be abandoned.
Entrusting this to manifest the perfect and eternal—how could one ever seek to distance oneself from it?
Though it is but a single luminous essence, its substance fully possesses the meaning of the three thousand realms;
according to the correct principle, it is internally contained within the faculties, objects, and consciousness, being complete therein.
Mind-only is indeed form-only; Fragrance-only, taste-only, touch-only, and sound-only as well.
This principle is worthy of careful reflection:
The natures of water and fire oppose one another, And light and darkness can mutually counteract each other.

the manifestation of their opposition reveals the possession of virtue. Those wise in contemplation perceive that this conformity expresses non-duality;

Observing the mental tendencies of beings, they are profound; At first glance, they seem like contradictory meanings, yet they emerge from the self-rotating *dhāraṇī*.
