[This is] the tenth question:
A doubt arises regarding the birth of those in the fruit of non-returning within the five Pure Abodes.
According to what is taught in the Hīnayāna, the fruit of non-returner (anāgāmiphala) encompasses all those noble ones who "stream upwards" (ūrdhvasrotas);
among them are those who are born in the five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa), namely the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala heavens.
Furthermore, since the body of one who has attained the fruit of non-returning does not perform karma for rebirth,
why is it that those in the lower three heavens can be born in the five Pure Abodes?
If it is said that one performs karma while at the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
then on the day of entering the state of rightness and departure from birth (samyaktva-niyāma),
one merely abandons the karma of ordinary-person maturation (vipāka).
How could an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) produce karma for rebirth in the five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*)?
Answer:
In the Hīnayāna, one enters the stage of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*) and abandons the delusions of vision (*dṛṣṭiheya*).
This refers precisely to the delusions that obstruct the principle [of reality].
First, one realizes the emptiness of persons and attains the mark of non-self.
Thus, one does not initiate karma,
thereby departing from the obstacles to the maturation-born [rebirth] in the four evil destinies.
As for its second fruit, it is the mixed dwelling of the five destinies within the desire realm.
The delusions that bind one to rebirth within the nine grades of realms and fetters lead to seven more births among humans and devas;
as for the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), it pertains to the form and formless realms.
The eighty-nine grades of delusions that moisten rebirth exist within the two realms of meditative concentration; since there are delusions to moisten rebirth,
one undergoes birth through the karma of those two realms.
Why would one doubt that they are born in the five Pure Abodes?
Only upon reaching the fourth fruit and permanently severing the fetters of the realms does one no longer undergo birth.

Answers to Chan Master Tai’s Ten Questions on the Buddha-Dharma; Answers to Chan Master Tai’s Ten Questions on the Buddha-Dharma, with Preface. Questioned by Chan Master Tai of the Chan School. Answered by Dharma Master Qing of Mingzhou. Qingtai has presumptuously occupied the gate of Chan.
Having the honor of accompanying the assembly of monks from all quarters,
I have observed the various points of doubt being deliberated;
I therefore venture to present ten questions.
I have specifically extended this request for further instruction.
I humbly beseech you:
you hold the golden surgical instrument in your hand.
I pray that you will treasure this mirror in your heart and deign to bring forth its brilliance,
so that it may forever serve as an excellent guide.
How great is my good fortune!
On the first day of the third month in the first year of the Tiānshèng era, Qīngtài questioned the Reverend Yánqìng, the Great Dharma Master Fǎzhì.
First Question:
Are ignorance and the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) sequential,
or are they non-sequential?
If one says there is a sequence of before and after,
how can it be said that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) has no beginning?
Ignorance likewise has no beginning.
Furthermore, it is asked:
"Is ignorance itself the Buddha-nature?"
If it is said that there is no sequence of before and after,
for what reason is it that within the state of Buddhahood,
ignorance is completely severed?
Only then does one attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Since it is said that [afflictions] are completely severed,
would this not imply that one must sever the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as well?
Answer:
If one discusses that which is fundamentally possessed,
the single nature of equality is neither true nor false.
Yet it does not speak of existence or non-existence;
it clarifies that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) likewise cannot be discussed in terms of having a beginning or an end.
It is simply that sentient beings, from time immemorial, have suddenly failed to awaken to it.
Delusion regarding principle gives rise to ignorance;
ignorance has the function of perfuming the True,
and the Dharma-nature has the capacity to follow along with the delusive.
The union of the real and the false is called dependent origination (pratyaya-utpāda).
Thus, the *Jinbi* states:
"There is no water without waves."
There is no wave that is not moist;
while existing within moisture, how could it be separate from the blending and clarity?
As a wave, it distinguishes itself as either clear or turbid.
Although there is clarity and turbidity, they are of one essence without distinction.
What is called the waves of clarity and turbidity refers to the dual functioning of the true and the false; the moist nature of clarity and turbidity is of one essence without distinction.
Because the dharma-nature of ignorance is a single essence, its arising has no before or after.
Thus, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"The Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit."
The characteristic of ignorance likewise has no beginning.
When one awakens, one realizes that the delusion is itself the truth;
one understands that ignorance is precisely the dharma-nature.
Speaking in terms of the gate of cultivation,
the meaning is that one should sever delusion.
Although it is said to "sever delusion," [it is not a matter of destroying something external].
The essence of delusion is fundamentally true;
what, then, is there to be severed within delusion?
Therefore it is said:
Ignorance likewise has no end.
Furthermore, if one investigates the moment of its correct delusion,
it is like a person in a dream.
Yet, unaware that this was a dream, one suddenly awakens from it;
delusion naturally subsides.
This is like the wind ceasing and the water becoming clear.
When delusion is eliminated, the truth is revealed.
Examine this carefully and reflect upon it;
there is no need for further discussion.
The second question:
All sentient beings are fundamentally of one and the same dharmatā;
this dharmatā is fundamentally pure.
For what reason and by what conditions did you suddenly become deluded?
Was it, for instance, at the very moment of initial delusion that you were deluded all at once?
This concerns confusion occurring either sequentially or simultaneously.
If one were to say that confusion occurs all at once,
then at the time of awakening, one should likewise awaken all at once and realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
Why is it that there are currently sentient beings who have not yet awakened?
If [the states of] before and after are identical in their single dharma-nature, [how can there be such a distinction]?
For what reason do these preceding and subsequent delusions arise?
Answer:
The virtuous, perfect, eternal, and correct nature of true emptiness and wondrous existence manifests when encountering conditions.
Such is the nature of things;
there is no need for contrived effort.
Now, as for the dependent origination of delusion and ignorance:
It is like a person who suddenly falls asleep;
while the spiritual flame is secretly present, the eyes perceive for only a moment before a deluded awakening suddenly arises.
Thus, all sentient beings are deluded regarding True Suchness (Tathatā), and that which causes the delusion remains unaware.
The union of the real and the false possesses the characteristic of non-duality between the two;
thus, although Buddha-nature is one,
and although delusion and awakening are identical.
Those in the six realms and four modes of birth encounter conditions that vary in their proximity to habitual tendencies;
their faculties and natures likewise differ in being either sharp or dull.
Therefore, there is a sequence between awakening and [ignorance].
It is certainly not the case that because the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and ignorance are one, the faculties and their natures must be identical.
Thus it is known.
All sentient beings are deluded without beginning or end,
yet awakening has a beginning and an end.
It is like many people sleeping together during the night.
Although they sleep at the same time,
it does not prevent them from waking up at different times;
understand this analogy well.
The questions that arise will naturally dissipate.
[He asked] three times:
"Since all sentient beings have already become deluded regarding their original nature,"
Why is it that one can suddenly attain awakening?
If you say that awakening is attained through the causal conditioning of the teachings of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra),
then what about the very first Buddha?
Furthermore, from whom did one obtain the faith, understanding, and awakening to the Dharma?
Answer:
Sentient beings attain awakening through different conditions of permeation (*vāsanā*).
There may be those who attain awakening spontaneously without a teacher,
realizing it by relying on their original, natural wisdom;
this is truly because they are inherently endowed with spiritual luminosity.
One is able to attain realization through one's own inferential reasoning.
Thus, the Patriarch said:
"Upon the body of emptiness and stillness, the wisdom that is not derived from a teacher can naturally be known."
Once one has realized one's own nature, one immediately becomes a Buddha.
After a single person has attained Buddhahood,
they propagate the Dharma in succession to transform deluded sentient beings.
Sentient beings receive the teachings and practice them;
therefore, they successively attain Buddhahood. If this is so, then...
Why do you doubt that the very first Buddha had no source from which he attained enlightenment?
Fourth question:
I have reverently heard that upon the fruition-stage of all Buddhas...
All dharmas realized by all beings are fully possessed by every sentient being.
For now, let us discuss this from the perspective of human beings within the causal stage:

how can one distinguish the functions of the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and even such feats as a hair swallowing the great ocean or a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru?
If one says that it is only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood that [this nature] is attained,
then what can be said regarding the doctrine of its primordial existence?
Answer:
Although the conditions for the arising of all Buddhas and sentient beings differ,
their ocean of awakening shares a common source.
All Buddhas awaken to this principle.
The nature and its characteristics are mutually unimpeded;
yet sentient beings, deluded and ignorant,
perceive phenomena and principle as being far removed from one another.
Therefore, the *Golden Scalpel* says:
"Sentient beings possess only the facts and principles within delusion;
the Buddhas possess both the facts and principles within awakening."
Although delusion and enlightenment differ,
the essence of phenomena and principle is one;
when a single Buddha attains the Way, [all are enlightened].
The Dharma-realm is nothing other than the environment and inhabitants of this Buddha;
it is sentient beings themselves who, within the Buddha’s environment and inhabitants,
give rise to suffering and joy, or ascent and descent.
Since the cycle of rising and sinking has already begun,
there is no foreseeable time for liberation;
now, by relying on the teachings to cultivate and refine oneself, one may accord with the perfect and ultimate truth.
One emulates what the Bodhisattvas practice:
the cultivation of non-action;
one accords with what the Buddhas have realized.
To realize that which is inherently present:
this means that in a single thought-moment, all things are suddenly perfected,
and all things are universally subsumed within a single speck of dust.
The three vidyās and eight liberations are never deficient in daily practice;
the five eyes and six supernormal powers are fully possessed in every moment.
Thus, Jingxi said:
Ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness;
form and fragrance are extinguished in purity.
The abode and its inhabitants of the Avīci Hell are entirely present within the self-mind of the ultimate sage.
The body and land of Vairocana are nothing other than the single thought-moment of an ordinary person;
that a hair swallows a mustard seed and contains it is the inconceivable great function of liberation of Vimalakīrti.
Moreover, even the single thought of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) that creates evil pervades the ten directions and the three periods of time;
how could the inconceivable great function not likewise encompass all?
If one does not believe that the mind of an ordinary person inherently possesses this function, [one fails to understand the nature of reality].
In that case, the mutual integration of the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*) upon the stage of the Buddhas' fruition would entirely fail to be established.
Fifth question:
Are the two dharmas of reality (*tattva*) and delusion (*mṛṣā*) identical or different?
If one says they are the same,
then since delusion is fundamentally the truth, the ancients should not have said that worldly wisdom is mistakenly taken for Buddha-wisdom—
like mistaking fish eyes for bright pearls.
If one were to say they are different,
then there would have to be a true reality existing apart from the false;
in that case, the ancients should not have said to "discard the waves to seek the water" or "abandon the vessel to seek the gold."
If both the real and the false are established yet do not coexist,
how can they be analyzed and explained?
Answer:
"To have both truth and delusion" refers to awakening as contrasted with confusion.
"To transcend both truth and delusion" refers to...
To obliterate appearances is to transcend the fishing trap;
to ascertain its essential meaning,
true reality is the truth that fully encompasses delusion.
Delusion is the delusion of the absolute reality;
the two have no dual essence.
When the Buddha, the Great Sage, speaks of reality and delusion, [he does so to reveal their non-duality].
Therefore, one desires people to admire the true and shatter all delusions,
so that delusions may not arise. Yet,
worldly people do not understand this point.
To insist that the deluded mind of the present moment is already the Buddha is precisely to fall into the error of the ancients who mistakenly identified [the Buddha] through forced recognition.
If one were to further discard this deluded thought and seek Tathatā elsewhere, [one would be lost].
Furthermore, this is identical to what is cultivated in the partial teachings;
it is like discarding the waves to seek the water, or abandoning the vessel to seek the gold.
Between these two extremes, one fault is no less than the other.
It is essential that one does not cling to nor depart from [reality], so that the wondrous is contained therein;
this is sufficient. This concludes the inquiry regarding the intent of the coming.
Regarding the identity or difference between the true and the false,
I now reply:
they do not exist within the categories of identity or difference.
This is a conventional designation of identity and difference.
That which is neither identical nor different is such because the true and the deluded share a single source, and bondage and liberation are non-dual.
The provisional establishment of similarity and difference refers to the disparity between delusion and enlightenment,
and the distinction between emotional consciousness and wisdom.
If one discriminates in this manner,
it will naturally accord with all the various texts;
there is no need for the trouble of an exhaustive discussion.
Sixth Question:

Now, regarding the statement that "insentient things preach the Dharma," does this mean that the fundamentally pure *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) itself is what preaches the Dharma for insentient things?
Does this mean that grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles preach the Dharma for those who are insentient?
If it is the fundamentally pure *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) that preaches the Dharma for the insentient,
then this nature extends horizontally across all things and penetrates vertically through all time.
Since the Buddha and sentient beings are equal,
one should not speak of the Dharma;
even if there were speech, it would be so.
Who is it that hears and receives?
If you point to grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles as those who preach the Dharma to the insentient,
how would you distinguish their doctrinal characteristics?
Answer:
The expression "insentient beings preach the Dharma" has its origins in antiquity.
Regarding the essentials of this treatise, its underlying intent is difficult to grasp.
Your question concerns establishing two distinct phenomena based on the pure dharma-nature (dharmatā): namely, grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles.
One should know that apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there are no separate tiles or wood;
apart from tiles and wood, there is no separate nature of phenomena.
These two are not two.
Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"The Dharma-nature pervades all places—every mountain, river, and land;
throughout the three periods of time, nothing remains excluded."
Furthermore, no form or characteristic can be apprehended therein.
If one were to discuss this Path in terms of having characteristics,
it would fill the vast emptiness of space.
It encompasses the Dharma-realm;
yet, when discussing the signless,
not a single dharma remains.
Seeing and hearing do not abide;
rolling up and unfolding are free and at ease;
the essence is revealed, majestic and grand.
In the past, when National Teacher Zhong of Nanyang answered a student's inquiry,
he stated that walls, tiles, and rubble are the heart-mind of the ancient Buddhas;
this is no different from the present teaching.
As for preaching the Dharma,
he taught with fervor and constancy,
without interruption from antiquity to the present.

Within the Avataṃsaka, there is the teaching of atoms, the teaching of lands, the teaching of Buddhas, the teaching of sentient beings, and the teaching of all things throughout the three periods of time.
As for its being heard and received,
it is taught simultaneously throughout the ten directions.
It is heard simultaneously throughout the ten directions;
it is proclaimed together across the three periods of time;
and it is heard together across the three periods of time.
An ancient said:
"Empty space questions the myriad phenomena;
the myriad phenomena answer empty space."
Who has personally heard it?
Muktaka, the youth of clear realization.
It is also said:
When he truly preached the Dharma, his voice did not manifest;
from the very center of the hall, his body vanished.
The student asked the National Teacher again:
"Who can hear the Dharma preached by insentient beings?
The Master replied,
"All Buddhas can hear it."
[The questioner] asked, "Should it not be that sentient beings have no [fixed] allotment?
The Master said,
"I speak for the sake of sentient beings."
[The monk] said, "I am deaf and blind and do not hear;
you, Master, ought to hear.
The Master said:
"I have not heard it either.
[The Master] said, "Since you, my teacher, have not heard it,
how can you know that insentient things preach the Dharma?"
The Master said,
"If I were to hear it,
I would be equal to all Buddhas."
"You would not hear the Dharma I preach.
He asked, "Will sentient beings ultimately hear it?
The Master said:
If sentient beings hear this,
they are no longer sentient beings;
the State Preceptor’s answer contains a subtle and profound significance.
The wise know this.
Seventh question:
How do sentient beings in the world transform into insentient things?
For example, the "Stone Lady," the earth-toad, and the stone-crab,
wherein insentient matter transforms into sentient beings;
or as wheat and withered grass transform into flying butterflies and fireflies.
By what causes and conditions do these classes of beings undergo such transformation?
Answer:
It is solely due to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Sentient beings manifest differently according to their karma.
For this reason, mountains, rivers, and the great earth are established, taking form through birth from a womb, an egg, moisture, or transformation.
As stated in the *Buddhāvatamsaka-sūtra* (Foding jing):
The nature of the ocean of awakening is tranquil and perfect;
this perfect tranquility makes awakening fundamentally subtle and wondrous.
Fundamental luminosity shines forth, giving rise to that which is perceived.
When that which was established ceases, the nature of illumination vanishes;
through delusion, empty space arises.
Depending upon this space, the world-system is established.
One's perceptions form the land;
one's cognitions constitute sentient beings.
Thus, that which is insentient is transformed into that which is sentient.
The divine consciousness arrives seizing its opportunity,
taking refuge in grass and clinging to wood; thus,
sentient beings transform insentient matter.
When the spiritual consciousness encounters the shifting transformations of the vital breath,
it drives away the husk and withers the decaying shell.
One should know that these thousand transformations do not depart from a single thought-moment.
The myriad transformations cannot escape the *ālayavijñāna*.
Furthermore, in this world, there are fire-mice, boiling insects, ice-silkworms, and stone-swallows;
the dimensions of sentient beings and their environments are difficult to measure.
How can the retribution of karma be fathomed?
That both the Buddha and sentient beings are equally inconceivable is seen herein.
This is the eighth question.
There are people in the world who,
while this body has not yet died,
have already been born in that place.
This is like the case of the king’s court officials and so forth.
What is the cause and condition for this?
If it is said that the karmic activity of sentient beings is sovereign, [then why is this not the case for them?]
All sentient beings possess karmic activity.
Why, then, is this not the case for [the Buddha]?
Answer:
Tiantai received from Nanyue three kinds of sublime dharmas:
first, the dharma of sentient beings;
second, the dharma of the Buddha.
The third is the mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).
Because these three are sublime,
they cannot be viewed with the eyes of cattle or sheep.
Furthermore, it cannot be fathomed by ordinary sentiments or worldly wisdom;
only those possessing the Tathāgata’s eye of wisdom are capable of measuring it.
This is truly because its essential nature is inconceivable, as each and every aspect is sublime and vast.
As stated in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha;
as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings.
The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—"
These three are without distinction;
it is because the Buddhas have wondrously realized the path of non-differentiation that they are able to manifest a thousand,
ten thousand, or a hundred million bodies from a single body.
From a single dharma, they manifest immeasurable dharmas; the great functioning of the six sense organs and three karmas within the dharma-realm is inexhaustible.
Although sentient beings dwelling in delusion cannot do so, [the Buddha can].
Because this essence and function are inherently complete within the nature-virtue,
one can manifest even a small portion of them within the very body of karmic retribution,
as was the case with Emperor Shun of antiquity.
He manifested his divided body to respond to the two consorts;
the spirit of the lady parted from her soul yet merged back into a single substance;
and the magistrate, while napping by day, recognized his own transformation into a fish.
There are even cases where two people remain together upon their pillows,
yet both spirits suffer calamities in hell;
such matters as these cannot be fully enumerated.
All these are inconceivable matters of karmic retribution within the realm of sentient beings.
Thus, one knows that it is not only the courtier Wang alone who experiences this;
why then do you labor under such bitter doubts and difficulties?
Question Nine:
Since sentient and insentient beings are of one and the same true nature,
why is it that trees are cut down?
One does not act as an adversary;
one does not cause others to fall into hell;
and one does not inflict even the slightest harm upon sentient beings.
This would then constitute an adversary;
why would it cause people to fall into suffering and receive retribution?
Furthermore, since both the primary and secondary retributions are of the same single dharma-nature, [how could they be opposed?]
For what reason do sentient beings possess cognition,
while insentient things lack cognition?
Answer:
The essence of the dharma-realm is free from all deluded thoughts;
its characteristics are like empty space,
pervading everywhere without exception.
Pervadingly relying upon and pervadingly corresponding with [the sense organs], pervadingly [engaging] the faculties and pervadingly [engaging] the objects,
down to a single atom, there is nothing that is not the entire dharma-dhātu pervading it.
Alas! All sentient beings are shackled by this physical body and delusively treat it as a vessel for emotions.
As for "emotions," they comprise the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence, whether moving through water, on land, or in the air.
As for "vessels," they comprise the mountains, rivers, peaks, and marshes, as well as the grasses, trees, and forests.
Within the realm of sentient beings, one falsely conceives of a self, persons, and cognitive views;
therefore, there arise matters of suffering, torment, and karmic retribution.
Since the realm of the vessel-world lacks such conceptions of a self, persons, and cognitive views, [such things do not exist].
Therefore, there is no karmic burden nor the transgression of seeking retribution for an enemy.
Such differences are all the deluded discriminations within the realm of sentient beings; when one investigates the ultimate reality of the *dharmadhātu*, they do not exist.
"What is the difference in their essential nature?
Therefore, Jingxi said:
"Even though one may create the basis or create the proper [image],..."
"Relying on principle, there is ultimately no divergent path;
these words are correct.
This concludes the tenth question.
Since all sentient beings share the same awakened nature,
for what reason do you strike others without feeling their pain?
Yet they are each joyful.
Since they do not know one another,
how can the nature of equal enlightenment be discerned?
Answer:
It is pure and fundamental;
there is not even a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind.
How much less need be said regarding the matter of the suffering of being beaten?
It is simply that True Suchness (tathatā) does not abide in its own nature,
but transforms into all phenomena (dharmas).
Just as water from a single source branches into different streams— some clear and some turbid, some still and some moving, the sea salty and rivers fresh—
so too among human beings do the notions of self and other arise in competition,
giving rise to likes and dislikes.
The strong oppress the weak,
and their attacks never cease.
Now, you have posed this question.
This is precisely a matter of weighing and discerning within delusion.
One should simply return from delusion to truth and turn away from dust to unite with awakening;

then one will realize that all sentient beings throughout the ten directions and three periods of time share a single Dharma-body, and that their single body, single wisdom, power, and fearlessness are likewise the same.
At this time, having realized the nature of equal enlightenment,
there is not even the mutual perception of the forms and characteristics of self and other.
How could one possibly discuss worldly matters such as beating or victory and defeat?

[End of] the second response to the three questions of Chan Master Tai. Chan Master Tai of the Chan School asks; Dharma Master Qingtai of Mingzhou answers: "I, Qingtai, do not presume upon my own ignorance. [End of] the second response to the three questions of Chan Master Tai."
I have previously submitted ten questions for your instruction;
I now receive your gracious reply.
Having read it three times, my heart was moved with emotion,
as if I had obtained a rare treasure.
Thus, the sun and moon are indeed luminous.
The blind man blames himself;
yet there remain three points therein that are not yet clear,
and I cannot help but again expose my own meager ignorance.
Having subsequently received your successive instructions, I,
Qingtai, feel the utmost gratitude for your compassion and report this to you,
the Great Dharma Master Fazhi, Preceptor of Yanqing Monastery.
I respectfully submit this first question.
In the first response, it says:
"Suddenly, one is unaware."
Delusion regarding principle gives rise to ignorance;
as for this very lack of awakening,
upon what does it depend for its arising?
What is its essence?
By what causes and conditions does it suddenly arise?
Answer:
The source of the profound *tathāgatagarbha* is neither true nor false;
yet this nature becomes true or false according to conditions (*pratyaya*).
Therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:
The absolute truth does not arise alone, and delusion cannot be established by itself;
it is only through the union of truth and delusion that anything can come to be.
Therefore, what is shown in the gates of teaching is that true existence has the meaning of remaining unchanging while following conditions,
whereas false existence has the capacity to manifest phenomena while its essence is empty.
This is truly because the numinous source abides nowhere.
It arises following delusion;
once the forced awakening has become confused,
it suddenly emerges.
However, regarding these words concerning the arising of delusion, one must further understand their intended meaning.
If it is said that the nature of sentient beings' fundamental enlightenment is perfectly luminous,
this directly points to the beginningless ignorance of sentient beings as being the dharma-nature.
Because the dharma-nature of ignorance is essentially one with it,
if one says that ignorance arises suddenly through non-awakening,
this is explained from the perspective of cultivation.
The discourse on nature arises from this.
It is not the case that non-awakening exists apart from the essence of original enlightenment.
Thus, one cannot manifest the path for those who advance in practice to return to their original nature and revert to the source.
It is for this reason that [the teaching] was established.
Most sutras and treatises generally state that delusion arises from the truth; however,
in reality, all sentient beings have, since beginningless time,
possessed nothing but delusive ignorance and a lack of awakening.
Therefore, the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states:
"All sentient beings are not called awakened because,
from the very beginning, they have never been separated from discursive thought."
This refers to beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikā-avidyā*).
You asked upon what non-enlightenment (*abodha*) depends for its arising;
if you understand the meaning above, [you will see].
Then it is not necessary to ask in this manner. For instance,
in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra, the son of Pūrṇa once harbored doubts regarding this matter,
and the Buddha rebuked him in return, saying:
Since it is called "delusion," how can it have a cause?
Furthermore, in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*, Vajragarbha also raises this same objection.
The Buddha rebuked this as not being a correct question.
Observing both instances closely,
it is clear that the Buddha’s true intention was not to give rise to such doubts and difficulties.
It is because the delusions of sentient beings have existed from the very beginning of the beginningless.
As stated in the second answer to the second question:
All sentient beings are deluded without beginning or end,
yet awakening has its beginning and end.
It is like many people sleeping together during the night.
Although they are the same at the time of sleep,
it does not hinder their awakening at different times;
if one awakens gradually in this manner, one will attain Buddhahood.
It would follow that there is a time when the realm of sentient beings comes to an end. If this were so,
why do the sūtras and śāstras both state that sentient beings are infinite?
Answer:
All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have obscured the Truth and given rise to various phenomenal appearances through their conjunction;
thus, although the source of Truth is non-dual, [appearances arise].
Yet that which is illuminated differs;
as an ancient worthy said:
"Sentient beings manifest according to their karma."
The three realms possess different forms,
like bubbles arising from water;
the water does not obstruct their sinking or floating.
Although the source of delusion is non-dual,
the process of perfuming and awakening gives rise to both the wise and the foolish.
Regarding your inquiry as to when the realm of sentient beings will be exhausted upon their attainment of Buddhahood:
It is like those water bubbles that arise from water;
although the bubbles perish one after another,
it cannot be said that the water perishes along with them.
Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states:
"In a single day, there are sentient beings as numerous as the sands of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Ganges Rivers who simultaneously attain Buddhahood."
The realm of sentient beings does not decrease,
nor does the realm of Buddhas increase. Why is this?
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is inexhaustible.
Furthermore, Master Changsha praised Nanquan, saying:
"Majestic and imposing, Nanquan is the source of the three generations."
The Vajra abides eternally and is inexhaustible throughout the ten directions;
its essential meaning is likewise the same.
One should contemplate this well.
One must by no means give rise to the view of annihilation within the inconceivable realm of sentient beings.
Thus ends the third question.
In the sixth answer, regarding the preaching of the Dharma by insentient things, it says:
Spoken simultaneously throughout the ten directions;
heard simultaneously throughout the ten directions;
proclaimed together across the three periods of time.
The three periods of time hear together.
Since they speak simultaneously,
how is it that they hear together?
